16  Text

Which point is which? text draws a string, a piece of text such as a name or a number, at each (x, y) position. It is point’s sibling: both place one glyph per row. A point’s glyph is a dot by default. A text mark’s glyph is a string, and that string comes from a column, through the label channel. This chapter uses it four ways: to name the points of a scatter, to print a value on a bar, to write a note on a plot, and to name the parts that a transform places, such as the nodes of a network.

Every plot in this chapter is drawn on a white panel, with theme(background = "white"), instead of gog’s light gray. Dark letters and gray dots are easier to read on white. The panel’s background shows the setting.

16.1 The mark and its content

A point tells you where a row is; it cannot tell you which row. The medals table holds five countries, one row each, with the number of gold, silver and bronze medals each country won. Drawn as dots, the five countries are five points with nothing to say which country is which:

medals: all 5 rows
country gold silver bronze
USA 46 37 38
China 38 31 22
Great Britain 29 17 19
Russia 19 18 9
Germany 17 10 15
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + point + x(gold) + y(silver) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Five countries, and no names") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(medals) + point + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Five countries, and no names") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(medals) + point + x(:gold) + y(:silver) + x_label("Gold") +
  y_label("Silver") + title("Five countries, and no names") +
  theme(background = "white")
plot(data(medals), point, x(col.gold), y(col.silver), x_label("Gold"),
  y_label("Silver"), title("Five countries, and no names"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given the medals: points, x is gold, y is silver.”

Replace point with text and bind label to country, and each row’s name is drawn at its position:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("The same five, named") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(medals) + text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("The same five, named") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(medals) + text + x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") + title("The same five, named") +
  theme(background = "white")
plot(data(medals), text, x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country),
  x_label("Gold"), y_label("Silver"), title("The same five, named"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given the medals: text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country.”

That is the main difference between the two marks. point draws the same dot at every row’s position. text draws one of the row’s own values there instead.

16.2 Both at once: the labeled scatter

A dot marks one position on the panel. A word is much wider than a dot, so a name on its own only shows roughly where its row is. The two marks can be drawn together: layer a point mark and a text mark on the same x and y, with the + operator. The dot gives the exact position and the string gives the name. That is a labeled scatter, built from two marks rather than a third mark of its own.

Each style() applies to the mark written before it. So style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") sets the dots’ size and colors them a medium gray. The words keep their own size and color. Without a nudge, each label is drawn centered on its dot, and the word hides the dot, as on the left. style(nudge = "up") moves every label above its dot, as on the right:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
((data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
    text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) +
    x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
    title("No nudge: each name sits on its dot") +
    theme(background = "white")) |
  (data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
     text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + style(nudge = "up") +
     x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
     title('nudge = "up": named just above') +
     theme(background = "white"))) +
  theme(width = 1000, height = 420)
(((data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
    text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) +
    x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
    title("No nudge: each name sits on its dot") +
    theme(background = "white")) |
  (data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
     text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) + style(nudge = "up") +
     x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
     title('nudge = "up": named just above') +
     theme(background = "white"))) +
  theme(width = 1000, height = 420))
((data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") + text +
  x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) + x_label("Gold") +
  y_label("Silver") + title("No nudge: each name sits on its dot") +
  theme(background = "white")) |
  (data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") + text +
  x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) + style(nudge = "up") +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("nudge = \"up\": named just above") +
  theme(background = "white"))) + theme(width = 1000, height = 420)
beside(plot(data(medals), point, style({ size: 5, color: "#9e9e9e" }),
  text, x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country), x_label("Gold"),
  y_label("Silver"), title("No nudge: each name sits on its dot"),
  theme({ background: "white" })),
  plot(data(medals), point, style({ size: 5, color: "#9e9e9e" }), text,
  x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country), style({ nudge: "up" }),
  x_label("Gold"), y_label("Silver"),
  title("nudge = \"up\": named just above"),
  theme({ background: "white" })), theme({ width: 1000, height: 420 }))

“Given the medals: points and also text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, beside points and also text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, with nudge up.”

16.2.1 Nudging the label off its point

Up is only one of four directions, and it is not always the side with room. A dot with a neighbor just above it has no space for its name there. Those labels need a different direction. style(nudge = ) shifts a text label off its (x, y). It takes one direction: "up", "down", "left", or "right":

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
(((data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
    text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + style(nudge = "up") +
    x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") + title('nudge = "up"') +
    theme(background = "white")) |
   (data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
     text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + style(nudge = "down") +
     x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") + title('nudge = "down"') +
     theme(background = "white"))) /
  ((data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
     text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + style(nudge = "left") +
     x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") + title('nudge = "left"') +
     theme(background = "white")) |
   (data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
     text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + style(nudge = "right") +
     x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") + title('nudge = "right"') +
     theme(background = "white")))) +
  theme(width = 1000, height = 760)
((((data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
    text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) + style(nudge = "up") +
    x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") + title('nudge = "up"') +
    theme(background = "white")) |
   (data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
     text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) + style(nudge = "down") +
     x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") + title('nudge = "down"') +
     theme(background = "white"))) /
  ((data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
     text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) + style(nudge = "left") +
     x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") + title('nudge = "left"') +
     theme(background = "white")) |
   (data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") +
     text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) + style(nudge = "right") +
     x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") + title('nudge = "right"') +
     theme(background = "white")))) +
  theme(width = 1000, height = 760))
(((data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") + text +
  x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) + style(nudge = "up") +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") + title("nudge = \"up\"") +
  theme(background = "white")) |
  (data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") + text +
  x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) + style(nudge = "down") +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") + title("nudge = \"down\"") +
  theme(background = "white"))) /
  ((data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") + text +
  x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) + style(nudge = "left") +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") + title("nudge = \"left\"") +
  theme(background = "white")) |
  (data(medals) + point + style(size = 5, color = "#9e9e9e") + text +
  x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) + style(nudge = "right") +

  theme(background = "white")))) + theme(width = 1000, height = 760)
below(beside(plot(data(medals), point,
  style({ size: 5, color: "#9e9e9e" }), text, x(col.gold), y(col.silver),
  label(col.country), style({ nudge: "up" }), x_label("Gold"),
  y_label("Silver"), title("nudge = \"up\""),
  theme({ background: "white" })),
  plot(data(medals), point, style({ size: 5, color: "#9e9e9e" }), text,
  x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country),
  style({ nudge: "down" }), x_label("Gold"), y_label("Silver"),
  title("nudge = \"down\""), theme({ background: "white" }))),
  beside(plot(data(medals), point, style({ size: 5, color: "#9e9e9e" }),
  text, x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country),
  style({ nudge: "left" }), x_label("Gold"), y_label("Silver"),
  title("nudge = \"left\""), theme({ background: "white" })),
  plot(data(medals), point, style({ size: 5, color: "#9e9e9e" }), text,
  x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country),
  style({ nudge: "right" }), x_label("Gold"), y_label("Silver"),
  title("nudge = \"right\""), theme({ background: "white" }))),
  theme({ width: 1000, height: 760 }))

“Given the medals: points and also text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, with nudge up, beside points and also text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, with nudge down; above points and also text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, with nudge left, beside points and also text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, with nudge right.”

You do not give a distance. The engine sets it from each label’s own font size, far enough that the word does not touch a dot of the default size. That is why nudge asks only for a direction, and every label moves in that one direction. jitter and dodge work differently: they compute each mark’s offset from the data, so marks can move by different amounts. Only text accepts a nudge. A point or a bar has no label to move, so the engine refuses the setting there and names the mark that does.

16.2.2 repel: moving labels off each other

A nudge shifts every label the same way, so it moves each label off its own dot and does nothing else. When the labels collide with each other, they all move together and still overlap. Thirty European countries are enough to show it. The gm_europe table holds them, one row per country in 2007, with each country’s GDP per person (gdp), life expectancy (life) and population:

gm_europe: first 5 of 30 rows
country continent year life population gdp
Albania Europe 2007 76.423 3600523 5937.030
Austria Europe 2007 79.829 8199783 36126.493
Belgium Europe 2007 79.441 10392226 33692.605
Bosnia and Herzegovina Europe 2007 74.852 4552198 7446.299
Bulgaria Europe 2007 73.005 7322858 10680.793
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_europe) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text + x(gdp) + y(life) + label(country) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Thirty countries, named") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(gm_europe) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + label(col.country) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Thirty countries, named") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(gm_europe) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") + text + x(:gdp) +
  y(:life) + label(:country) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("Thirty countries, named") +
  theme(background = "white")
plot(data(gm_europe), point, style({ color: "#9e9e9e" }), text,
  x(col.gdp), y(col.life), label(col.country), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("Thirty countries, named"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given gapminder Europe: points and also text, x is gdp, y is life, label by country.”

Every name is centered on its own dot, and where the countries crowd together the words overlap. Germany, Belgium, Finland and the United Kingdom have almost the same gdp and life, so their four names are drawn on top of one another.

repel solves that. It is one of the four collision modifiers, with jitter, dodge and stack, so it is written after the mark with *, not inside style(). It measures where the labels and the dots actually are, then moves each label off the words around it:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_europe) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text * repel + x(gdp) + y(life) + label(country) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same thirty, moved apart") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(gm_europe) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text * repel + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + label(col.country) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The same thirty, moved apart") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(gm_europe) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") + text * repel +
  x(:gdp) + y(:life) + label(:country) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("The same thirty, moved apart") +
  theme(background = "white")
plot(data(gm_europe), point, style({ color: "#9e9e9e" }),
  layer(text, repel), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), label(col.country),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The same thirty, moved apart"), theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given gapminder Europe: points and also text derived by repel, x is gdp, y is life, label by country.”

Notice three things in this plot. Every label is drawn just outside its dot, so no word covers the dot it names. A label with other words near it moves to whichever side has room. A label with space around it stays directly above its dot. The first two follow from one rule: repel pulls each label toward its own dot, and pushes it away from every other word and every dot, its own included. The third follows from where repel starts. A plain label is centered on its dot, but repel starts every label just above its dot, so a label with nothing near it stays there.

In a more crowded plot, repel can move a label much further from its dot. Once the gap is larger than the height of one line of text, gog draws a thin line from the dot to the word, so you can still see which dot the name belongs to. No label in this plot moved that far, so none has a line.

The placement is deterministic. It uses no random-number generator and does not read the computer’s clock, so the same sentence draws the same picture every time. It does depend on the order of the rows, though. repel settles the overlaps pair by pair, in the order of the rows, so the same rows in a different order can end with some labels in different places.

Sometimes no placement keeps every label apart. repel then still draws every label, and gog prints a message saying how many still overlap. Which names to leave out is your decision, so repel never removes one. In this plot all thirty fit, so gog prints no message.

gapminder_2007 holds the same columns as gm_europe for all 142 countries in 2007:

gapminder_2007: first 5 of 142 rows
country continent year life population gdp
Afghanistan Asia 2007 43.828 31889923 974.5803
Albania Europe 2007 76.423 3600523 5937.0295
Algeria Africa 2007 72.301 33333216 6223.3675
Angola Africa 2007 42.731 12420476 4797.2313
Argentina Americas 2007 75.320 40301927 12779.3796

The same sentence with this table names all 142 countries, and they do not all fit. In theme(), grid = "none" also leaves out the gridlines, so they do not run through the crowded labels:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text * repel + x(gdp) + y(life) + label(country) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("All 142 countries, named") +
  theme(background = "white", grid = "none")
(data(gapminder_2007) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text * repel + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + label(col.country) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("All 142 countries, named") +
  theme(background = "white", grid = "none"))
data(gapminder_2007) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") + text * repel +
  x(:gdp) + y(:life) + label(:country) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") + title("All 142 countries, named") +
  theme(background = "white", grid = "none")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, style({ color: "#9e9e9e" }),
  layer(text, repel), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), label(col.country),
  x_label("GDP per person"), y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("All 142 countries, named"),
  theme({ background: "white", grid: "none" }))
gog: 3 of 142 labels still overlap another one after `repel` moved them — there is no arrangement of this many words that fits this panel. Every label was drawn, so none is missing; they are crowded. A larger plot (`theme(width =, height =)`), a smaller `style(size = )`, or fewer rows in the layer separates them.

“Given gapminder 2007: points and also text derived by repel, x is gdp, y is life, label by country.”

Every country is named, but three labels still overlap another one, and the message says so. Many labels moved far from their dots, so gog drew a thin line from each of those dots to its name.

Three things give crowded labels more room, and the message names all three: fewer rows, a smaller style(size = ), and a larger plot. theme(width =, height =) sets the plot’s size in pixels, and the Composition chapter explains it.

Fewer rows is often the right choice. On a large table you usually name only the few rows that matter: give the text layer its own table that holds just those rows, as A note is a layer does with one row. In the web edition, clicking a dot on a plot with brush() shows its values beside it, which Selection calls a stamp. Stamps help you choose those rows. A stamp is gone when the page reloads, while a text label is part of the sentence and is drawn every time.

In the next plot, the dots come from gapminder_2007 again. The names come from gm_populous, the ten countries with the most people in 2007. It has the same columns, so the text layer reads gdp and life from it:

gm_populous: first 5 of 10 rows
country continent year life population gdp
China Asia 2007 72.961 1318683096 4959.115
India Asia 2007 64.698 1110396331 2452.210
United States Americas 2007 78.242 301139947 42951.653
Indonesia Asia 2007 70.650 223547000 3540.652
Brazil Americas 2007 72.390 190010647 9065.801
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  data(gm_populous) + text * repel + label(country) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The ten most populous of 142 countries, named") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(gapminder_2007) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  data(gm_populous) + text * repel + label(col.country) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The ten most populous of 142 countries, named") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(gapminder_2007) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) + data(gm_populous) + text * repel +
  label(:country) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("The ten most populous of 142 countries, named") +
  theme(background = "white")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, style({ color: "#9e9e9e" }),
  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life), data(gm_populous),
  layer(text, repel), label(col.country), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("The ten most populous of 142 countries, named"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, and also text from the ten most populous countries, derived by repel, label by country.”

The gdp axis uses a log scale (Scales), which gives the many poorer countries more room. repel moves the names off the 132 unnamed dots too, though the dots and the names come from different tables. It moves a name off those dots only a little, never far enough for gog to draw a thin line. So a name can still cover some of them: United States covers several at the top right, and Bangladesh covers two. A halo keeps such a name readable.

A nudge and repel can be used together, and each does one job. style(nudge = ) chooses the side each label is pulled toward, and repel then moves the labels that still overlap:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_europe) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text * repel + x(gdp) + y(life) + label(country) + style(nudge = "right") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Nudged right first, then moved apart") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(gm_europe) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  text * repel + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + label(col.country) + style(nudge = "right") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Nudged right first, then moved apart") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(gm_europe) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") + text * repel +
  x(:gdp) + y(:life) + label(:country) + style(nudge = "right") +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Nudged right first, then moved apart") +
  theme(background = "white")
plot(data(gm_europe), point, style({ color: "#9e9e9e" }),
  layer(text, repel), x(col.gdp), y(col.life), label(col.country),
  style({ nudge: "right" }), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"),
  title("Nudged right first, then moved apart"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given gapminder Europe: points and also text derived by repel, x is gdp, y is life, label by country, with nudge right.”

With every label pulled to the right of its dot, four labels run into their neighbors there, and repel moves those four far enough to need a thin line. Norway’s dot is at the right edge of the panel. repel keeps every label inside the panel, and unlike a plain label it does not widen the axis to make room. So Norway’s label is moved back over its own dot.

16.3 Number labels: the value on each mark

A label does not have to be a name, and it does not have to be drawn on a scatter. A bar shows which country won more gold medals. To read how many more, a reader has to measure each bar against the axis, and that measurement is only an estimate. Sometimes the number itself is the answer. Bind a column that holds numbers and each row’s value is drawn. By default, a whole number is printed without a decimal point, and any other number is rounded to at most three decimal places. Layer text over bar to print each bar’s height. Without a nudge, each number is centered on its bar’s top edge, and the edge crosses the digits. style(nudge = "up") moves each number just above its bar:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + bar + style(color = "steelblue") +
  text + x(country) + y(gold) + label(gold) + style(nudge = "up") +
  y_label("Gold medals") +
  title("Each bar labeled with its height") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(medals) + bar + style(color = "steelblue") +
  text + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) + label(col.gold) + style(nudge = "up") +
  y_label("Gold medals") +
  title("Each bar labeled with its height") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(medals) + bar + style(color = "steelblue") + text + x(:country) +
  y(:gold) + label(:gold) + style(nudge = "up") + y_label("Gold medals") +
  title("Each bar labeled with its height") + theme(background = "white")
plot(data(medals), bar, style({ color: "steelblue" }), text,
  x(col.country), y(col.gold), label(col.gold), style({ nudge: "up" }),
  y_label("Gold medals"), title("Each bar labeled with its height"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given the medals: bars and also text, x is country, y is gold, label by gold, with nudge up.”

Each bar now carries its number, so the difference between the USA’s 46 and China’s 38 can be read without the axis.

The medals table already holds the numbers. A bar chart that counts rows computes its numbers itself. In bar * count, the count transform writes the number of rows in each bar into a column called count. text * count uses the same transform, so label(count) can print that column on each bar. The count column is not in gapminder_2007. The transform writes it, so only a layer that runs the transform can name it. The column each transform writes lists the column each transform writes. As in the medals plot, the numbers are nudged up:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) +
  text * count + label(count) + style(nudge = "up") +
  title("Each bar labeled with its count") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent) +
  text * count + label(col.count) + style(nudge = "up") +
  title("Each bar labeled with its count") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent) + text * count +
  label(:count) + style(nudge = "up") +
  title("Each bar labeled with its count") + theme(background = "white")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent),
  layer(text, count), label(col.count), style({ nudge: "up" }),
  title("Each bar labeled with its count"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, x is continent, and also text derived by count, label by count, with nudge up.”

Africa’s bar is labeled 52, and Oceania’s bar is labeled 2.

To draw the bars horizontally, put the category on y instead of x. Each bar is then drawn from left to right, and the counts are on the x axis. The text layer reads the same positions, so each number is centered on the right end of its bar. The nudge points in the direction the bars grow, so it is now style(nudge = "right"), which moves each number just past that end:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + y(continent) +
  text * count + label(count) + style(nudge = "right") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + y(col.continent) +
  text * count + label(col.count) + style(nudge = "right") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + y(:continent) + text * count +
  label(:count) + style(nudge = "right") + theme(background = "white")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), y(col.continent),
  layer(text, count), label(col.count), style({ nudge: "right" }),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by count, y is continent, and also text derived by count, label by count, with nudge right.”

Africa’s 52 is past the end of the longest bar, and Oceania’s 2 is past the shortest. The axis already reaches a little past the longest bar, and Africa’s 52 fits in that room. A label that would not fit inside the panel widens its axis instead (Scales).

A histogram is labeled the same way. The bin transform also writes a column called count, the number of rows in each bin. So text * bin with label(count) prints how many countries fall in each bin of life expectancy:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(life) +
  text * bin + label(count) + style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(col.life) +
  text * bin + label(col.count) + style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin + x(:life) + text * bin + label(:count) +
  style(nudge = "up") + theme(background = "white")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin), x(col.life), layer(text, bin),
  label(col.count), style({ nudge: "up" }),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin, x is life, and also text derived by bin, label by count, with nudge up.”

The last bin, from about 78 to 83 years, holds the most countries: 32.

Add proportion to both layers, and each bar is a share of all the countries instead of a count. bin writes a count column, and proportion then turns each count into a share, so the rows hold a column called proportion and no count. The text layer therefore names label(proportion):

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * proportion + x(life) +
  text * bin * proportion + label(proportion, decimals = 2) +
  style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * proportion + x(col.life) +
  text * bin * proportion + label(col.proportion, decimals = 2) +
  style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * proportion + x(:life) +
  text * bin * proportion + label(:proportion, decimals = 2) +
  style(nudge = "up") + theme(background = "white")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin, proportion), x(col.life),
  layer(text, bin, proportion), label(col.proportion, { decimals: 2 }),
  style({ nudge: "up" }), theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin and proportion, x is life, and also text derived by bin and proportion, label by proportion with 2 decimal places, with nudge up.”

The last bin is now labeled 0.23. Its 32 countries make a share of 0.2254 of the 142, and decimals = 2 rounds the share to two decimal places. decimals is explained a few plots below, where each continent’s mean life expectancy is printed. These rows hold no count, so label(count) is refused, and the message names the transform that replaced it:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * proportion + x(life) +
  text * bin * proportion + label(count)
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * proportion + x(col.life) +
  text * bin * proportion + label(col.count))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * proportion + x(:life) +
  text * bin * proportion + label(:count)
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin, proportion), x(col.life),
  layer(text, bin, proportion), label(col.count))
Error:
! gog: `label(count)` names the `count` that `bin` writes, and `proportion` then turns each count into a share, so the rows `text * bin * proportion` draws hold `proportion` and no `count`. `label(proportion)` reads the share. To read the counts, drop `proportion` from every layer that has it.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

After count, bin or proportion there is one row for each bar. A label can print only a column those rows hold. In bar * count + x(continent), those rows hold two columns, count and continent. Each row is a whole continent, so it holds no country to print:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(continent) +
  text * count + label(country)
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(col.continent) +
  text * count + label(col.country))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * count + x(:continent) + text * count +
  label(:country)
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, count), x(col.continent),
  layer(text, count), label(col.country))
Error:
! gog: `label(country)` names a column of your table, and `text * count` replaces your rows with its own, one for each `continent`, which have no `country`. `label(count)` prints each count, and `label(continent)` names each one.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

After a summary such as mean, there is also one row for each bar. In bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life), each of those rows holds its continent’s mean, written into life itself. A summary is given a column to reduce, here the life named on y, so its answer replaces that column. count, bin and proportion are given no column, so they write a new column with a name of their own. So text * mean with label(life) prints each continent’s mean life expectancy:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
  text * mean + label(life) + style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  text * mean + label(col.life) + style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  text * mean + label(:life) + style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), layer(text, mean), label(col.life), style({ nudge: "up" }),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life, and also text derived by mean, label by life, with nudge up.”

Asia’s mean, 70.72848, is printed as 70.728. For sum, median, max, min and quantile, write label() with the column the summary reads.

Asia’s label, 70.728, has more decimal places than this plot needs. You cannot round a mean before gog computes it, so label() takes the number of decimal places to print. label(life, decimals = 1) prints Asia’s mean as 70.7:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(continent) + y(life) +
  text * mean + label(life, decimals = 1) + style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) +
  text * mean + label(col.life, decimals = 1) + style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * mean + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  text * mean + label(:life, decimals = 1) + style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, mean), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), layer(text, mean), label(col.life, { decimals: 1 }),
  style({ nudge: "up" }), theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by mean, x is continent, y is life, and also text derived by mean, label by life with 1 decimal place, with nudge up.”

Each label now has one decimal place, from Africa’s 54.8 to Oceania’s 80.7. Every label gets exactly one decimal place, so a mean of exactly 77 would print as 77.0, and all five labels show the same precision. decimals = 0 rounds each mean to a whole number, so Asia’s prints as 71. gog reads a categorical column as names, not numbers, so there is no number to round, and label(country, decimals = 1) is refused:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country, decimals = 1)
data(medals) + text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country, decimals = 1)
data(medals) + text + x(:gold) + y(:silver) +
  label(:country, decimals = 1)
plot(data(medals), text, x(col.gold), y(col.silver),
  label(col.country, { decimals: 1 }))
Error:
! gog: `label(country, decimals = 1)`: `country` is read as categories, names rather than numbers, so there is no number to round. Leave `decimals` out. If its values are numbers, make the column numeric in the host language first.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

A sum can be a very large number. bar * sum with y(population) adds up the people of each continent, and label(population) prints Asia’s sum in full, as 3811953827. A number that long is hard to read. label(population, short = TRUE) prints it short, with K for thousands, M for millions, B for billions (a thousand millions) and T for trillions (a million millions):

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum + x(continent) + y(population) +
  text * sum + label(population, short = TRUE) + style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum + x(col.continent) + y(col.population) +
  text * sum + label(col.population, short = True) + style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum + x(:continent) + y(:population) +
  text * sum + label(:population, short = true) + style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, sum), x(col.continent),
  y(col.population), layer(text, sum),
  label(col.population, { short: true }), style({ nudge: "up" }),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by sum, x is continent, y is population, and also text derived by sum, label by population written short, with nudge up.”

Asia’s label is now 3.81B, and Oceania’s is 24.5M. A short number keeps three significant digits. decimals sets the number of decimal places instead, so label(population, short = TRUE, decimals = 1) prints 3.8B for Asia. An axis takes short too: y(population, short = TRUE) takes each tick’s letter from the tick’s own size, as Scales shows. Without short, an axis chooses one letter for all its ticks from the distance between them. Here the ticks are a billion apart, so the axis already writes 1B, 2B, 3B and 4B, and short would change nothing.

A share can be printed as a percent. label(proportion, percent = TRUE) prints the last bin’s share, 0.2254, as 22.5%:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * proportion + x(life) +
  y(proportion, percent = TRUE) +
  text * bin * proportion + label(proportion, percent = TRUE) +
  style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * proportion + x(col.life) +
  y(col.proportion, percent = True) +
  text * bin * proportion + label(col.proportion, percent = True) +
  style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * proportion + x(:life) +
  y(:proportion, percent = true) + text * bin * proportion +
  label(:proportion, percent = true) + style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin, proportion), x(col.life),
  y(col.proportion, { percent: true }), layer(text, bin, proportion),
  label(col.proportion, { percent: true }), style({ nudge: "up" }),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin and proportion, x is life, y is proportion written as a percent, and also text derived by bin and proportion, label by proportion written as a percent, with nudge up.”

The axis takes the same argument on y(proportion), so the axis and the labels are written the same way. Without decimals, a percent keeps one decimal place and leaves it off when it is 0, so a share of 0.190 prints as 19%, not 19.0%. percent and short cannot be used together, because they are two ways to write one number. The message asks you to keep one of them:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * proportion + x(life) +
  text * bin * proportion + label(proportion, percent = TRUE, short = TRUE)
(data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * proportion + x(col.life) +
  text * bin * proportion + label(col.proportion, percent = True, short = True))
data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * proportion + x(:life) +
  text * bin * proportion +
  label(:proportion, percent = true, short = true)
plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin, proportion), x(col.life),
  layer(text, bin, proportion),
  label(col.proportion, { percent: true, short: true }))
Error:
! gog: `label(proportion)` asks for both `short` and `percent`, two ways to write one number. Keep one of them.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

label() prints a column of dates as dates, such as 2024-03-01, and a column of date-times with the hour and minute, such as 2024-03-01 14:05. A date is not written as a number, so gog refuses decimals, short and percent on it.

After bin * cumulative, each bin holds two numbers: its own count, and the total so far. cumulative writes the total to a column named cumulative, and the count column that bin wrote stays beside it. So label(cumulative) prints the height of each bar, and label(count) prints each bin’s own count on the same bar:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * cumulative + x(life) +
    text * bin * cumulative + label(cumulative) + style(nudge = "up") +
    title("label(cumulative): the running total") +
    theme(background = "white")) |
   (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * cumulative + x(life) +
      text * bin * cumulative + label(count) + style(nudge = "up") +
      title("label(count): each bin on its own") +
      theme(background = "white"))) +
  theme(width = 1000, height = 420)
(((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * cumulative + x(col.life) +
    text * bin * cumulative + label(col.cumulative) + style(nudge = "up") +
    title("label(cumulative): the running total") +
    theme(background = "white")) |
   (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * cumulative + x(col.life) +
      text * bin * cumulative + label(col.count) + style(nudge = "up") +
      title("label(count): each bin on its own") +
      theme(background = "white"))) +
  theme(width = 1000, height = 420))
((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * cumulative + x(:life) +
  text * bin * cumulative + label(:cumulative) + style(nudge = "up") +
  title("label(cumulative): the running total") +
  theme(background = "white")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + bar * bin * cumulative + x(:life) +
  text * bin * cumulative + label(:count) + style(nudge = "up") +
  title("label(count): each bin on its own") +
  theme(background = "white"))) + theme(width = 1000, height = 420)
beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin, cumulative),
  x(col.life), layer(text, bin, cumulative), label(col.cumulative),
  style({ nudge: "up" }), title("label(cumulative): the running total"),
  theme({ background: "white" })),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(bar, bin, cumulative), x(col.life),
  layer(text, bin, cumulative), label(col.count), style({ nudge: "up" }),
  title("label(count): each bin on its own"),
  theme({ background: "white" })), theme({ width: 1000, height: 420 }))

“Given gapminder 2007: bars derived by bin and cumulative, x is life, and also text derived by bin and cumulative, label by cumulative, with nudge up, beside bars derived by bin and cumulative, x is life, and also text derived by bin and cumulative, label by count, with nudge up.”

The bars, and the places of the labels, are the same in both plots, because x and y place a label and label chooses only the number it shows. On the left, each number is the bar’s height, so it matches the y axis: the last bar reaches 142. On the right, the numbers do not match the y axis, and that is not a mistake. Each is the count of one bin: 32, the last, is 142 minus the 110 before it.

16.3.1 Labels on dodged bars

With dodge, grouped bars set one bar per group side by side in each slot, the stretch of the axis that belongs to one category. A label layer without dodge prints all of a slot’s numbers in its middle, between the bars. With the same dodge and a split of its own, each label is printed on its own bar. The gm_eras table holds two years, 1957 and 2007, with one row per country in each:

gm_eras: first 5 of 284 rows
country continent year life population gdp era
Afghanistan Asia 1957 30.332 9240934 820.8530 1957
Afghanistan Asia 2007 43.828 31889923 974.5803 2007
Albania Europe 1957 59.280 1476505 1942.2842 1957
Albania Europe 2007 76.423 3600523 5937.0295 2007
Algeria Africa 1957 45.685 10270856 3013.9760 1957

color(era) is written after bar, so it colors the bars alone (Encoding scope). group(era) splits the labels by era without coloring them:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
  text * mean * dodge + group(era) + label(life, decimals = 1) +
  style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + color(col.era) +
  text * mean * dodge + group(col.era) + label(col.life, decimals = 1) +
  style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  color(:era) + text * mean * dodge + group(:era) +
  label(:life, decimals = 1) + style(nudge = "up") +
  theme(background = "white")
plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, mean, dodge), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), color(col.era), layer(text, mean, dodge), group(col.era),
  label(col.life, { decimals: 1 }), style({ nudge: "up" }),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given the gapminder eras: bars derived by mean and dodge, x is continent, y is life, colored by era, and also text derived by mean and dodge, grouped by era, label by life with 1 decimal place, with nudge up.”

Each continent has two labels, one on each era’s bar. Africa’s 41.3 is on its 1957 bar, and its 54.8 is on its 2007 bar. A text layer with dodge is refused when nothing splits it, because it then has no groups to set side by side. color(era) belongs to the bars alone, so without group(era) the text layer has no split. The message names color and group as the two ways to add one:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(continent) + y(life) + color(era) +
  text * mean * dodge + label(life, decimals = 1)
(data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + color(col.era) +
  text * mean * dodge + label(col.life, decimals = 1))
data(gm_eras) + bar * mean * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  color(:era) + text * mean * dodge + label(:life, decimals = 1)
plot(data(gm_eras), layer(bar, mean, dodge), x(col.continent),
  y(col.life), color(col.era), layer(text, mean, dodge),
  label(col.life, { decimals: 1 }))
Error:
! gog: `text * dodge` has no groups to set side by side — nothing splits the mark. Add `color(<field>)` or `group(<field>)` so there are groups to dodge.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

16.3.2 Labels on stacked bars

With stack, the groups are piled up in one bar instead of being set side by side, so each group is one segment of the bar. Only the lowest segment can be read from the y axis, because each other segment starts where the one below it ends. A label layer with the same stack and a split of its own prints each segment’s value in the middle of that segment. The titanic table counts the people on the Titanic by class, sex, age and whether they survived, with one row for each combination and the count in n:

titanic: first 5 of 32 rows
class sex age survived n
1st Male Adult Yes 57
1st Male Adult No 118
1st Male Child Yes 5
1st Male Child No 0
1st Female Adult Yes 140

The plot adds up n for each class. As in the dodged plot, color(survived) is written after bar, so it splits only the bars, into the people who survived and the people who did not. group(survived) splits the labels the same way, without coloring them. A third layer, text * sum with no split, adds up all of a class’s rows, so it prints the class’s total. style(nudge = "up", size = 18) moves that total above the bar and draws it larger than the labels inside the segments:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(titanic) + bar * sum * stack + x(class) + y(n) + color(survived) +
  text * sum * stack + group(survived) + label(n) +
  text * sum + label(n) + style(nudge = "up", size = 18) +
  y_label("People") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(titanic) + bar * sum * stack + x(col["class"]) + y(col.n) + color(col.survived) +
  text * sum * stack + group(col.survived) + label(col.n) +
  text * sum + label(col.n) + style(nudge = "up", size = 18) +
  y_label("People") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(titanic) + bar * sum * stack + x(:class) + y(:n) + color(:survived) +
  text * sum * stack + group(:survived) + label(:n) + text * sum +
  label(:n) + style(nudge = "up", size = 18) + y_label("People") +
  theme(background = "white")
plot(data(titanic), layer(bar, sum, stack), x(col.class), y(col.n),
  color(col.survived), layer(text, sum, stack), group(col.survived),
  label(col.n), layer(text, sum), label(col.n),
  style({ nudge: "up", size: 18 }), y_label("People"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given titanic: bars derived by sum and stack, x is class, y is n, colored by survived, and also text derived by sum and stack, grouped by survived, label by n, and text derived by sum, label by n, with nudge up and size 18.”

Each label prints the number of people in its own segment. Of the 885 crew members, 212 survived. The upper segment holds the 673 who did not survive. It ends at 885 on the y axis, but its label prints 673, the people in that segment alone. stack moves each segment up to where the one below it ends, and the label still prints the segment’s own count. No segment’s label shows the class’s total, so the third layer prints it above the bar.

As with dodge, a text layer with stack on the default baseline is refused when nothing splits it, because it then has no groups to pile up. The message names color and group as the two ways to add one:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(titanic) + bar * sum * stack + x(class) + y(n) + color(survived) +
  text * sum * stack + label(n)
(data(titanic) + bar * sum * stack + x(col["class"]) + y(col.n) + color(col.survived) +
  text * sum * stack + label(col.n))
data(titanic) + bar * sum * stack + x(:class) + y(:n) + color(:survived) +
  text * sum * stack + label(:n)
plot(data(titanic), layer(bar, sum, stack), x(col.class), y(col.n),
  color(col.survived), layer(text, sum, stack), label(col.n))

16.4 Color

You see a hue faster than you can read a word, so a color split shows you the groups before you read a single name. Every label so far has been printed in one color, which is the default. Map a categorical column to color and the labels split by that column. A continuous column on color is refused on a text mark, and the message suggests size or opacity instead, as What it refuses shows. The mapping gets a legend to name the groups, and the colors come from the same palette that points and bars use. In the plot below, which draws the medals table shown in The mark and its content, each country is its own group, so the hue repeats the name. style(size = 15) draws the letters a little larger than the default 13 pixels, as Styling: one color, one size explains:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + color(country) +
  style(size = 15) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("One hue per country") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(medals) + text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) + color(col.country) +
  style(size = 15) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("One hue per country") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(medals) + text + x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) +
  color(:country) + style(size = 15) + x_label("Gold") +
  y_label("Silver") + title("One hue per country") +
  theme(background = "white")
plot(data(medals), text, x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country),
  color(col.country), style({ size: 15 }), x_label("Gold"),
  y_label("Silver"), title("One hue per country"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given the medals: text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, color by country, with size 15.”

The legend names the five hues. A column whose value several rows share, such as continent, is more useful: one hue marks every name in a group before you read any of them. The gm_populous table, shown in repel: moving labels off each other, has such a column. Its ten countries come from three continents:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gm_populous) + text * repel + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  label(country) + color(continent) +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(gm_populous) + text * repel + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  label(col.country) + color(col.continent) +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(gm_populous) + text * repel + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  label(:country) + color(:continent) + theme(background = "white")
plot(data(gm_populous), layer(text, repel), x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), label(col.country), color(col.continent),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given the ten most populous countries: text derived by repel, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life, label by country, color by continent.”

The six Asian names share one hue, the three from the Americas share another, and Nigeria is the only name in a third hue.

16.5 Styling: one color, one size

The color channel takes its hues from a column. When the words are the whole plot, with no dots or bars beside them, you may want one color of your own and a larger font. The default size, 13 pixels, is often too small to read comfortably. Neither comes from a column, so both are settings rather than mappings. style(color = ) sets the color of the words, and style(size = ) sets the font size in pixels. Each applies to every label in the layer:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) +
  style(color = "seagreen", size = 17) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Bigger, greener labels") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(medals) + text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) +
  style(color = "seagreen", size = 17) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Bigger, greener labels") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(medals) + text + x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) +
  style(color = "seagreen", size = 17) + x_label("Gold") +
  y_label("Silver") + title("Bigger, greener labels") +
  theme(background = "white")
plot(data(medals), text, x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country),
  style({ color: "seagreen", size: 17 }), x_label("Gold"),
  y_label("Silver"), title("Bigger, greener labels"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given the medals: text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, colored seagreen, with size 17.”

A setting gives every label in the layer the same font size. To size each label by a value of its own, map a column instead, as the next section shows.

16.6 Sizing and fading labels by a column

size and opacity are channels on text, as they are on point. A mapped size draws each label at a font size from 8 to 24 pixels. The smallest value gets 8, the largest gets 24, and the others fall in proportion between them. Here, the more bronze medals a country won, the larger its name:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + size(bronze) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Each name sized by its bronze medals") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(medals) + text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) + size(col.bronze) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Each name sized by its bronze medals") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(medals) + text + x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) +
  size(:bronze) + x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Each name sized by its bronze medals") +
  theme(background = "white")
plot(data(medals), text, x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country),
  size(col.bronze), x_label("Gold"), y_label("Silver"),
  title("Each name sized by its bronze medals"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given the medals: text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, size by bronze.”

The legend shows the letter a at three sizes between 8 and 24 pixels, because a label is read by the size of its letters. A mapped opacity works the same way. The smallest value is drawn at opacity 0.15, faint but visible, and the largest at 0.95:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + opacity(bronze) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Fewer bronze medals, fainter name") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(medals) + text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) + opacity(col.bronze) +
  x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Fewer bronze medals, fainter name") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(medals) + text + x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) +
  opacity(:bronze) + x_label("Gold") + y_label("Silver") +
  title("Fewer bronze medals, fainter name") + theme(background = "white")
plot(data(medals), text, x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country),
  opacity(col.bronze), x_label("Gold"), y_label("Silver"),
  title("Fewer bronze medals, fainter name"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given the medals: text, x is gold, y is silver, label by country, opacity by bronze.”

These two plots show that size and opacity work on text as they do on point, not that they suit this table. Size is hard to read on words, because a long name looks larger than a short one at the same font size, and a faint name is hard to read at all. To compare bronze medals, a position such as x(bronze), or the number itself, as in Number labels, shows them more clearly.

gog sets each channel’s scale from every row of the layer, so one value draws at the same size and opacity in every panel.

A word cloud also sizes each word by a value, but its positions carry no data: each word is placed wherever there is room. In gog a label is drawn at its row’s x and y, and repel only moves it off its neighbors, so gog draws no word cloud.

16.7 Labels in the cube

A 3-D scatter has the same problem as a flat one: a dot does not say which row it is. A label can be drawn in the cube, as a point can. Bind z, and each label is drawn at the place its row’s three positions give it. Nearer labels are drawn over farther ones:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + point + text * repel + x(gold) + y(silver) + z(bronze) +
  label(country) + title("Each country at its three medal counts") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(medals) + point + text * repel + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + z(col.bronze) +
  label(col.country) + title("Each country at its three medal counts") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(medals) + point + text * repel + x(:gold) + y(:silver) + z(:bronze) +
  label(:country) + title("Each country at its three medal counts") +
  theme(background = "white")
plot(data(medals), point, layer(text, repel), x(col.gold), y(col.silver),
  z(col.bronze), label(col.country),
  title("Each country at its three medal counts"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given the medals: points and also text derived by repel, x is gold, y is silver, z is bronze, label by country.”

repel moves labels off each other and off the dots, as on a flat plot. A nudge moves a label on the picture, not in the cube: "up" is toward the top of the image at every angle.

In the web edition, turn the cube with the pointer, as Three measurements on three axes shows: drag left and right to turn it, and up and down to tip it. At every angle repel places the labels again, so you can watch each name move away from the other names and from the dots.

16.8 A halo around each label

A label drawn over a dot or a line can be hard to read, because the mark shows around its letters. style(border_size = ) draws a halo: a band of the panel’s background color around each letter, drawn under the text. It hides the mark next to each letter and does not change the letters. The ten most populous countries, from the gm_populous table shown in repel: moving labels off each other, have names that cross other countries’ dots. Here they are without a halo and with one. Neither plot draws the life axis, so the two are the same size and repel puts every name in the same place in both:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
((data(gapminder_2007) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
    x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life, axis = FALSE) +
    data(gm_populous) + text * repel + label(country) +
    x_label("GDP per person") + title("No halo") +
    theme(background = "white", grid = "none")) |
   (data(gapminder_2007) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
      x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life, axis = FALSE) +
      data(gm_populous) + text * repel + label(country) +
      style(border_size = 2) +
      x_label("GDP per person") + title("Names with a halo") +
      theme(background = "white", grid = "none"))) +
  theme(width = 1100, height = 460)
(((data(gapminder_2007) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
    x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life, axis = False) +
    data(gm_populous) + text * repel + label(col.country) +
    x_label("GDP per person") + title("No halo") +
    theme(background = "white", grid = "none")) |
   (data(gapminder_2007) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
      x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life, axis = False) +
      data(gm_populous) + text * repel + label(col.country) +
      style(border_size = 2) +
      x_label("GDP per person") + title("Names with a halo") +
      theme(background = "white", grid = "none"))) +
  theme(width = 1100, height = 460))
((data(gapminder_2007) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life, axis = false) + data(gm_populous) +
  text * repel + label(:country) + x_label("GDP per person") +
  title("No halo") + theme(background = "white", grid = "none")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + point + style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life, axis = false) + data(gm_populous) +
  text * repel + label(:country) + style(border_size = 2) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + title("Names with a halo") +
  theme(background = "white", grid = "none"))) +
  theme(width = 1100, height = 460)
beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, style({ color: "#9e9e9e" }),
  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life, { axis: false }),
  data(gm_populous), layer(text, repel), label(col.country),
  x_label("GDP per person"), title("No halo"),
  theme({ background: "white", grid: "none" })),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, style({ color: "#9e9e9e" }),
  x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }), y(col.life, { axis: false }),
  data(gm_populous), layer(text, repel), label(col.country),
  style({ border_size: 2 }), x_label("GDP per person"),
  title("Names with a halo"),
  theme({ background: "white", grid: "none" })),
  theme({ width: 1100, height: 460 }))

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life without an axis, and also text from the ten most populous countries, derived by repel, label by country, beside points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life without an axis, and also text from the ten most populous countries, derived by repel, label by country, with border size 2.”

On the left, the dots behind United States, Mexico and Brazil show through their letters. On the right, a thin band of the panel’s color separates every letter from the dots behind it. border_size sets the width, in pixels, of the line drawn around each letter to make the halo. Half of that line lies under the letters, so a width of 2 shows as a band 1 pixel wide. border_color sets its color, if you want one other than the background. Either setting alone draws a halo: an unset width is 3 pixels, and an unset color is the panel’s background color. With neither, a label has no halo.

repel moves a name off dots that have no name only a little, and a nudge would move every name the same way, often onto other dots. A halo makes each name readable where it is. It also suits a label that has to stay where it is: a note written along the line it describes, as in Turning a label, or the name of a network node with edges passing behind it, as in Transforms it takes.

A halo hides the marks it covers, so use it where the words matter more than those marks. Within one layer it never hides another label’s letters, because every halo in a layer is drawn before any of that layer’s letters. A text layer written later is drawn on top, so its halos can cover the letters of an earlier text layer. A halo does not move overlapping labels apart. That is the job of repel.

16.9 Turning a label

A note beside a vertical line is easiest to read when it is written along the line, not across it. style(angle = ) turns every label in its layer by the number of degrees you give, counterclockwise from horizontal, so 90 reads upward and -90 downward. Each label turns around its own position, the point its x and y give. The milestones table holds two notes. Each is drawn at the income in at and the height in value:

milestones: all 2 rows
at value note
10000 72 less steep from here
40000 80 almost flat here

In this plot a vertical rule marks each income, and each note is drawn along its rule:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp, scale = "log") + y(life) +
  style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  data(milestones) + rule + x(at) + style(color = "steelblue") +
  data(milestones) + text + x(at) + y(value) + label(note) +
  style(angle = 90, border_size = 2) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Notes turned 90 degrees") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp, scale = "log") + y(col.life) +
  style(color = "#9e9e9e") +
  data(milestones) + rule + x(col.at) + style(color = "steelblue") +
  data(milestones) + text + x(col.at) + y(col.value) + label(col.note) +
  style(angle = 90, border_size = 2) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Notes turned 90 degrees") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp, scale = "log") + y(:life) +
  style(color = "#9e9e9e") + data(milestones) + rule + x(:at) +
  style(color = "steelblue") + data(milestones) + text + x(:at) +
  y(:value) + label(:note) + style(angle = 90, border_size = 2) +
  x_label("GDP per person") + y_label("Life expectancy") +
  title("Notes turned 90 degrees") + theme(background = "white")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp, { scale: "log" }),
  y(col.life), style({ color: "#9e9e9e" }), data(milestones), rule,
  x(col.at), style({ color: "steelblue" }), data(milestones), text,
  x(col.at), y(col.value), label(col.note),
  style({ angle: 90, border_size: 2 }), x_label("GDP per person"),
  y_label("Life expectancy"), title("Notes turned 90 degrees"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp on a log scale, y is life; then given the milestones: rules, x is at; then given the milestones: text, x is at, y is value, label by note, with angle 90.”

Each note is now parallel to its line, and the halo from the section above hides the line behind its letters. The two notes do not crowd each other, so the plot needs no repel. Where turned labels do crowd, text * repel keeps them apart: repel measures each label by the space it takes after turning.

Where a transform places each name inside a region, gog fits the name for you. A sunburst turns or shrinks a name that does not fit its sector, and a nest shrinks it. A flow draws every name at full size, so a long name may need style(angle = 90) to fit its tall, narrow slot.

16.10 Why label is a channel

A setting is a value you type into the sentence. You might expect to type a label into the sentence in the same way, like a title. A label is not a title: it is one value per row, and that makes it data. One rule of the grammar decides whether a label is a setting or a channel: data reaches a mark only through a channel. That makes label a channel, so no mark takes the words themselves as an argument. A fixed note is therefore a table with one row, given to data(), and never a value given to style().

Only text accepts label; every other mark refuses it, which is why a labeled scatter is point + text and never a label on point. text requires a label: the label is part of the mark’s minimum syllable, as x and y are. Ask for a text mark with no label and the engine refuses, and says what to write instead, as What it refuses shows. text is the mark, and label is the channel that carries the column it draws.

16.11 A note is a layer

A plot often needs one note written on it, at a place you choose. It may say what a region of the scatter means, or why a point is where it is. If you have used ggplot2, a note there is a separate function, annotate(). In gog it is a table with one row, and the plot below draws it. A second data() gives the mark written right after it its own table (Data), and a table with one row in it puts one string on the plot:

income_note: its one row
gdp life what
35000 66 high income, short lives
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(gdp) + y(life) +
  data(income_note) + text + label(what) +
  title("A note is a layer, not a function") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) +
  data(income_note) + text + label(col.what) +
  title("A note is a layer, not a function") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(gapminder_2007) + point + x(:gdp) + y(:life) + data(income_note) +
  text + label(:what) + title("A note is a layer, not a function") +
  theme(background = "white")
plot(data(gapminder_2007), point, x(col.gdp), y(col.life),
  data(income_note), text, label(col.what),
  title("A note is a layer, not a function"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given gapminder 2007: points, x is gdp, y is life, and also text from the income note, label by what.”

The note is in an empty corner of the scatter: no country in 2007 has an income that high with lives that short.

That plot needed nothing new in the grammar. A mark written directly after a data() already reads that table, and text already draws one string per row. The note is data like any other, so it is scaled like any other. Give the note an x far from the points, and the axes stretch to cover it, so check the axes each time you place a note.

That is more to write than ggplot2’s annotate(): a table, even for one note. In return, a note follows every rule a row follows. It is placed on the axes’ scale, it can take channels such as color, several notes are rows of one table, and one table can feed several layers, as milestones feeds a rule and a text in Turning a label.

One rule applies while writing a note. The text layer names no position of its own, so it reads the columns the axes use, gdp and life, from its own table. That is why income_note has a column with each of those names. When a note table’s columns have other names, write its positions after text, as Turning a label does for the milestones table: + text + x(at) + y(value) + label(note). Any other mark at a place you choose is written the same way: a small table, and a layer over it. A dot on the plot is a point over the same one-row table, and several notes are several rows.

16.12 Text that a transform places

You choose where a note goes. A transform can choose the place instead, and then the text names whatever that transform built. The table’s first three transforms, layout, flow and partition, are explained in later chapters, so you do not need to know them yet: the table only shows where a label can go. In the first seven rows, a second layer with the same transform draws the shape that the text names:

Text derived by What it labels
text * layout the nodes of a network, beside point * layout and edge * layout (Network)
text * flow each stage’s slots in a flow, beside ribbon * flow and zone * flow (Flow)
text * partition the regions of a hierarchy, beside zone * partition (Polar)
text * count, text * bin the count of each bar, beside bar * count or bar * bin (Number labels)
text * mean, text * sum and the other summaries the summary of each bar, beside bar * mean or bar * sum (Number labels)
text * dodge each group’s bar in a slot, beside bar * dodge (Labels on dodged bars)
text * stack each group’s segment of a pile, beside bar * stack (Labels on stacked bars)
text * repel the scatter labels of repel, moved off each other

The plots in Transforms it takes, below, draw the first three, one at a time. In each, the text is a layer over the mark that drew the shape, and both layers read the same transform.

16.13 Transforms it takes

A transform computes new values from the rows, and the mark draws those values instead of the rows. The table lists, by kind, the transforms a text mark takes and the ones it refuses:

Kind Takes Refuses
Counting bin, count, density, proportion —
Summaries sum, mean, median, max, min, quantile —
Fitted lines — smooth, straight
Running total cumulative —
Pairs: a low and a high — range, confidence, deviation, smooth_band, straight_band, bounds
Collision modifiers dodge, stack, repel jitter
Layouts of a whole picture partition, flow, layout cluster

The plots below show every transform a text mark takes. Within a figure the plots differ mainly in their transform, and the paragraph before each figure names any other change. Every text layer needs label(). After a transform, the label can print only a column that the new rows hold, as Number labels explains.

Counting. count and proportion tally the rows at each value of x, on a category or a number. bin counts the rows in each interval of a number, and density estimates, as a smooth curve, how closely the rows lie along it. Each one writes its result into a column, count, proportion or density, and label() prints that column. Each puts its result on the axis you leave empty, so a larger count is printed higher. The left and middle plots put continent on x, and the right plot puts life. decimals = 2 prints each proportion to two decimal places:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
(data(gapminder_2007) + text * count + x(continent) + label(count) +
   title("text * count") +
   theme(background = "white")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + text * proportion + x(continent) +
     label(proportion, decimals = 2) + title("text * proportion") +
     theme(background = "white")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + text * bin + x(life) + label(count) +
     title("text * bin") +
     theme(background = "white"))
((data(gapminder_2007) + text * count + x(col.continent) + label(col.count) +
   title("text * count") +
   theme(background = "white")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + text * proportion + x(col.continent) +
     label(col.proportion, decimals = 2) + title("text * proportion") +
     theme(background = "white")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + text * bin + x(col.life) + label(col.count) +
     title("text * bin") +
     theme(background = "white")))
(data(gapminder_2007) + text * count + x(:continent) + label(:count) +
  title("text * count") + theme(background = "white")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + text * proportion + x(:continent) +
  label(:proportion, decimals = 2) + title("text * proportion") +
  theme(background = "white")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + text * bin + x(:life) + label(:count) +
  title("text * bin") + theme(background = "white"))
beside(beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(text, count),
  x(col.continent), label(col.count), title("text * count"),
  theme({ background: "white" })),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(text, proportion), x(col.continent),
  label(col.proportion, { decimals: 2 }), title("text * proportion"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(text, bin), x(col.life),
  label(col.count), title("text * bin"), theme({ background: "white" })))

“Given gapminder 2007: text derived by count, x is continent, label by count, beside text derived by proportion, x is continent, label by proportion with 2 decimal places, beside text derived by bin, x is life, label by count.”

density gets a figure of its own. The curve is computed at 256 places unless you set places, so the left plot prints 256 numbers. They cover each other, and together they draw the shape of the curve rather than numbers you can read. On the right, density(places = 12) computes it at 12 places, and each number is the curve’s height at one of them:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
((data(gapminder_2007) + text * density + x(life) +
    label(density, decimals = 3) + title("text * density") +
    theme(background = "white")) |
   (data(gapminder_2007) + text * density(places = 12) + x(life) +
      label(density, decimals = 3) + title("text * density(places = 12)") +
      theme(background = "white"))) +
  theme(width = 1100, height = 460)
(((data(gapminder_2007) + text * density + x(col.life) +
    label(col.density, decimals = 3) + title("text * density") +
    theme(background = "white")) |
   (data(gapminder_2007) + text * density(places = 12) + x(col.life) +
      label(col.density, decimals = 3) + title("text * density(places = 12)") +
      theme(background = "white"))) +
  theme(width = 1100, height = 460))
((data(gapminder_2007) + text * density + x(:life) +
  label(:density, decimals = 3) + title("text * density") +
  theme(background = "white")) |
  (data(gapminder_2007) + text * density(places = 12) + x(:life) +
  label(:density, decimals = 3) + title("text * density(places = 12)") +
  theme(background = "white"))) + theme(width = 1100, height = 460)
beside(plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(text, density), x(col.life),
  label(col.density, { decimals: 3 }), title("text * density"),
  theme({ background: "white" })),
  plot(data(gapminder_2007), layer(text, density({ places: 12 })),
  x(col.life), label(col.density, { decimals: 3 }),
  title("text * density(places = 12)"), theme({ background: "white" })),
  theme({ width: 1100, height: 460 }))

“Given gapminder 2007: text derived by density, x is life, label by density with 3 decimal places, beside text derived by density at 12 places, x is life, label by density with 3 decimal places.”

A curve is easier to read as a stroke, line * density, as the density section of Transforms shows.

Summaries. The six summaries reduce the rows at each value of x to one value, so they need a number on y. sum reads population, because only an amount has a total that means something. The other five read life. They give the mean, the median, the largest and the smallest value, and quantile(0.9) gives the value that nine tenths of the rows fall below. A summary writes its value into the column it reads, so label() names that column: label(population, short = TRUE) after sum, and label(life, decimals = 1) after the other five. Each label is drawn above a bar with the same summary, moved up by style(nudge = "up"). That is the usual way to label a summary:

(((data(gapminder_2007) + bar * sum + x(continent) + y(population) +

The five plots that read life share one scale, so their bars can be compared from plot to plot, and each label prints the value, to one decimal place.

Running total. cumulative adds each value to the ones before it along the axis. It writes the total to a column named cumulative, and label(cumulative) prints it. The actuals table holds one year of sales in each row:

actuals: all 5 rows
year sales
2019 120
2020 135
2021 128
2022 152
2023 168

  • Python
  • Julia
