data(actuals) + text * cumulative + x(year) + y(sales) + label(cumulative) +
  title("text * cumulative") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(actuals) + text * cumulative + x(col.year) + y(col.sales) + label(col.cumulative) +
  title("text * cumulative") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(actuals) + text * cumulative + x(:year) + y(:sales) +
  label(:cumulative) + title("text * cumulative") +

plot(data(actuals), layer(text, cumulative), x(col.year), y(col.sales),
  label(col.cumulative), title("text * cumulative"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given the actuals: text derived by cumulative, x is year, y is sales, label by cumulative.”

The last label, 703, is the total of all five years. The rows still hold each year’s own sales, so label(sales) would print 168 at the same place.

With start_from = "previous", cumulative places each label halfway between the total before its item and the total after it. That is the middle of the item’s bar in a waterfall chart. The income table is an income statement (a company’s revenue and its costs), with one row for each item, and amount holds each item’s own number:

income: all 6 rows
item amount
Revenue 500
Cost of goods -290
Operating costs -130
Interest -10
Other income 15
Tax -20

  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(income) + text * cumulative(start_from = "previous") + x(item) + y(amount) +
  label(amount) + x_label("") +
  title('text * cumulative(start_from = "previous")') +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(income) + text * cumulative(start_from = "previous") + x(col.item) + y(col.amount) +
  label(col.amount) + x_label("") +
  title('text * cumulative(start_from = "previous")') +

data(income) + text * cumulative(start_from = "previous") + x(:item) +
  y(:amount) + label(:amount) + x_label("") +
  title("text * cumulative(start_from = \"previous\")") +
  theme(background = "white")
plot(data(income), layer(text, cumulative({ start_from: "previous" })),
  x(col.item), y(col.amount), label(col.amount), x_label(""),
  title("text * cumulative(start_from = \"previous\")"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given the income table: text derived by cumulative starting from the previous total, x is item, y is amount, label by amount.”

Each label prints its item’s own amount, at the middle of the bar that bar * cumulative(start_from = "previous") draws. The cost of goods takes 290 from the revenue of 500, so its label, -290, is printed at 355, halfway between 500 and 210. Bar draws the bars under the labels.

Collision modifiers. Collision modifiers move marks that would be drawn on top of one another. dodge sets the groups in one slot side by side, and stack piles them up in one bar, so both need a split, such as color or group. The top plot prints each continent’s mean life expectancy in 1957 and in 2007, from the gm_eras table shown in Labels on dodged bars. The middle plot prints how many people in each class of the Titanic survived and how many did not, from the titanic table shown in Labels on stacked bars. No bars are drawn here, but each label is still where the middle of its segment would be. repel moves each label off the other labels. The bottom plot names the ten countries of gm_populous, shown in repel: moving labels off each other, with gdp on x and life on y:

    theme(background = "white")) /
   (data(titanic) + text * sum * stack + x(class) + y(n) + color(survived) +
      label(n) + title("text * sum * stack") +
      theme(background = "white")) /

      title("text * repel") +
      theme(background = "white"))) +
  theme(height = 1350)
(((data(gm_eras) + text * mean * dodge + x(col.continent) + y(col.life) + color(col.era) +
    label(col.life, decimals = 1) + title("text * mean * dodge") +
    theme(background = "white")) /
   (data(titanic) + text * sum * stack + x(col["class"]) + y(col.n) + color(col.survived) +
      label(col.n) + title("text * sum * stack") +
      theme(background = "white")) /
   (data(gm_populous) + text * repel + x(col.gdp) + y(col.life) + label(col.country) +
      title("text * repel") +
      theme(background = "white"))) +
  theme(height = 1350))
((data(gm_eras) + text * mean * dodge + x(:continent) + y(:life) +
  color(:era) + label(:life, decimals = 1) +
  title("text * mean * dodge") + theme(background = "white")) /
  (data(titanic) + text * sum * stack + x(:class) + y(:n) +
  color(:survived) + label(:n) + title("text * sum * stack") +
  theme(background = "white")) /
  (data(gm_populous) + text * repel + x(:gdp) + y(:life) +
  label(:country) + title("text * repel") +

below(below(plot(data(gm_eras), layer(text, mean, dodge),
  x(col.continent), y(col.life), color(col.era),
  label(col.life, { decimals: 1 }), title("text * mean * dodge"),
  theme({ background: "white" })),
  plot(data(titanic), layer(text, sum, stack), x(col.class), y(col.n),

“Given the gapminder eras: text derived by mean and dodge, x is continent, y is life, color by era, label by life with 1 decimal place; above text from titanic, derived by sum and stack, x is class, y is n, color by survived, label by n; above text from the ten most populous countries, derived by repel, x is gdp, y is life, label by country.”

Layouts. partition, flow and layout each work out where every part of the picture goes. For partition the parts are the regions of a hierarchy, for flow the slots of each stage, and for layout the nodes of a network. Each transform writes the name of every part into a new column, name. A text layer with the same transform prints those names with label(name), each at the place where another layer draws its part. The three plots below show one transform each.

partition splits a whole into nested parts, such as a budget into groups and items, so it needs a hierarchy of categorical columns. The spending table holds a household budget, with the money spent on each item in amount:

spending: first 5 of 12 rows
group item detail amount
Housing Rent NA 980
Housing Utilities Energy 140
Housing Utilities Water 35
Housing Repairs NA 120
Food Groceries NA 420
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(spending) + x(amount) + zone * partition(group, item) + color(group) +
  style(border_color = "white", border_size = 2) +
  text * partition(group, item) + label(name) + style(angle = 90) +
  title("text * partition, with the zones") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(spending) + x(col.amount) + zone * partition(col.group, col.item) + color(col.group) +
  style(border_color = "white", border_size = 2) +
  text * partition(col.group, col.item) + label(col.name) + style(angle = 90) +
  title("text * partition, with the zones") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(spending) + x(:amount) + zone * partition(:group, :item) +
  color(:group) + style(border_color = "white", border_size = 2) +
  text * partition(:group, :item) + label(:name) + style(angle = 90) +
  title("text * partition, with the zones") + theme(background = "white")
plot(data(spending), x(col.amount),
  layer(zone, partition(col.group, col.item)), color(col.group),
  style({ border_color: "white", border_size: 2 }),
  layer(text, partition(col.group, col.item)), label(col.name),
  style({ angle: 90 }), title("text * partition, with the zones"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given the spending table: x is amount, zones derived by partition through group and item, colored by group, with border color white and border size 2, and also text derived by partition through group and item, label by name.”

zone * partition(group, item) draws a rectangle for each group along the bottom and one for each item above its group, each as wide as its share of amount. The name column holds both kinds of name, so label(name) prints each group’s name, such as Housing, in its rectangle along the bottom, and each item’s name, such as Rent, in its rectangle above. An item has its group’s color, so style(border_color = "white", border_size = 2) draws a white edge around every rectangle to show where each one ends. The names are turned with style(angle = 90), as in Turning a label, so that each fits its narrow rectangle.

flow splits an amount at each of a series of stages, such as each person’s class on the Titanic and then whether they survived, so it needs one column for each stage. This plot uses the titanic table, shown in Labels on stacked bars, and sizes each part by n on y. A reader compares the thickness of the bands and the slots rather than reading numbers, so axis = FALSE, grid = "none" and frame = "none" leave out the count axis, the gridlines and the frame, as in Leaving out the count axis and the grid:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(titanic) + y(n, axis = FALSE) + ribbon * flow(class, survived) +
  color(class) +
  zone * flow(class, survived) + text * flow(class, survived) +
  label(name) + title("text * flow, with the bands and the slots") +
  theme(grid = "none", frame = "none", background = "white")
(data(titanic) + y(col.n, axis = False) + ribbon * flow(col["class"], col.survived) +
  color(col["class"]) +
  zone * flow(col["class"], col.survived) + text * flow(col["class"], col.survived) +
  label(col.name) + title("text * flow, with the bands and the slots") +
  theme(grid = "none", frame = "none", background = "white"))
data(titanic) + y(:n, axis = false) + ribbon * flow(:class, :survived) +
  color(:class) + zone * flow(:class, :survived) +
  text * flow(:class, :survived) + label(:name) +
  title("text * flow, with the bands and the slots") +
  theme(grid = "none", frame = "none", background = "white")
plot(data(titanic), y(col.n, { axis: false }),
  layer(ribbon, flow(col.class, col.survived)), color(col.class),
  layer(zone, flow(col.class, col.survived)),
  layer(text, flow(col.class, col.survived)), label(col.name),
  title("text * flow, with the bands and the slots"),
  theme({ grid: "none", frame: "none", background: "white" }))

“Given titanic: y is n without an axis, ribbons derived by flow through class and survived, colored by class, and also zones derived by flow through class and survived, and text derived by flow through class and survived, label by name.”

zone * flow(class, survived) draws a slot for each class on the left and one for each answer, Yes or No, on the right, and ribbon * flow draws the bands between them. The text prints Crew in the middle of the Crew slot and No in the middle of the No slot. The bands have no names. Instead, color(class), written after ribbon, gives each band the color of the class it starts from, and the legend names the colors. Follow the 3rd class band, and most of it ends in No.

layout is for tables that record relations rather than measurements: each row says that one name is related to another, and no column gives a name a position. So layout computes a position for each name, and it needs two columns of names and the network space, network(). The trade_partners table has one row for each trade relation, naming who exports and who imports, with the value of the goods and the exporter’s continent:

trade_partners: first 5 of 22 rows
exporter importer billions continent
China United States 500 Asia
Mexico United States 455 Americas
Canada United States 420 Americas
United States Mexico 320 Americas
United States Canada 355 Americas
  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(exporter, importer) +
  text * layout(exporter, importer) + label(name) +
  style(border_size = 2) + network() +
  title("text * layout, with the edges") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) +
  text * layout(col.exporter, col.importer) + label(col.name) +
  style(border_size = 2) + network() +
  title("text * layout, with the edges") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(trade_partners) + edge * layout(:exporter, :importer) +
  text * layout(:exporter, :importer) + label(:name) +
  style(border_size = 2) + network() +
  title("text * layout, with the edges") + theme(background = "white")
plot(data(trade_partners),
  layer(edge, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)),
  layer(text, layout(col.exporter, col.importer)), label(col.name),
  style({ border_size: 2 }), network(),
  title("text * layout, with the edges"), theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given trade partners: edges derived by layout from exporter to importer, and also text derived by layout from exporter to importer, label by name, in the network.”

layout gives each country a position, and edge * layout draws a line between two positions for each trade relation. No other mark is drawn at a position, so the name itself shows where the country is: China is printed where the lines to its seven trade partners meet. The names have a halo, which hides the lines behind their letters.

A text mark refuses every transform in the Refuses column of the table at the start of this section. smooth and straight compute a line at evenly spaced places along x, not at the values in your rows. A label there would print no value from your table. A line draws the fitted values instead. The pair transforms give y a low and a high at each value of x, two numbers where a label prints one. interval and ribbon draw the pair, and text * max or text * min prints one end of a range. jitter moves each point a short way along the categorical axis, and it does not measure the space a label’s letters take, so jittered labels can still cover each other. repel does measure it, so it is the collision modifier that moves labels apart. cluster joins the closest categories into a tree, which path draws.

16.14 What you can set

The Styling section set a color and a size. Those are two entries in a longer list, and the whole of it is here: which color, how transparent, which size, which way to shift the label, by how many degrees to turn it, and the color and width of its halo. A setting gives one value to every label in the layer. Three of them, color, size and opacity, can instead be mapped from a column, as the sections above show. Each mark takes its own settings. Setting vs mapping shows how a setting differs from mapping a column. These are a text mark’s settings, with the values each accepts:

Setting Value
style(color = ) any CSS color name or hex
style(opacity = ) 0 to 1
style(size = ) pixels
style(border_color = ) any CSS color name or hex
style(border_size = ) pixels
style(nudge = ) up, down, left, right
style(angle = ) degrees, counterclockwise from horizontal

nudge and angle are the two settings only text has. nudge exists so a layered point + text does not draw the label on top of the dot. The plot uses the medals table, shown in The mark and its content:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + x(country) + y(gold) +
  point + style(color = "#9e9e9e", size = 6) +
  text + label(gold) + style(nudge = "up", size = 11, color = "black") +
  y_label("Gold medals") + title("Labels nudged off their points") +
  theme(background = "white")
(data(medals) + x(col.country) + y(col.gold) +
  point + style(color = "#9e9e9e", size = 6) +
  text + label(col.gold) + style(nudge = "up", size = 11, color = "black") +
  y_label("Gold medals") + title("Labels nudged off their points") +
  theme(background = "white"))
data(medals) + x(:country) + y(:gold) + point +
  style(color = "#9e9e9e", size = 6) + text + label(:gold) +
  style(nudge = "up", size = 11, color = "black") +
  y_label("Gold medals") + title("Labels nudged off their points") +
  theme(background = "white")
plot(data(medals), x(col.country), y(col.gold), point,
  style({ color: "#9e9e9e", size: 6 }), text, label(col.gold),
  style({ nudge: "up", size: 11, color: "black" }),
  y_label("Gold medals"), title("Labels nudged off their points"),
  theme({ background: "white" }))

“Given the medals: x is country, y is gold, points colored #9e9e9e, with size 6, and also text, label by gold, colored black, with nudge up and size 11.”

Each count is just above its dot, and neither covers the other. The four directions, and how far a nudge moves a label, are under Nudging the label off its point, with repel for labels that collide with each other.

The grid of every mark and every setting shows which other marks share this list. What a mark maps rather than sets is its row on the grid of marks and channels.

16.15 What it refuses

A text mark always refuses four things: a missing label, the shape channel, any pattern, and a continuous column on color. It refuses group only when no statistic, no dodge and no stack uses it. The label is part of the mark’s minimum syllable, as x and y are: with no string, a text mark has nothing to draw. The engine refuses and names the channel to add:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver)
data(medals) + text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver)
data(medals) + text + x(:gold) + y(:silver)
plot(data(medals), text, x(col.gold), y(col.silver))
Error:
! gog: `text` needs `label()` but none is set. Add `label(<column>)` — a text cannot be drawn without it.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

A reader who knows point will try its channels on text. size and opacity draw with a continuous column, as on a point. color draws only with a categorical column, unlike a point, which takes either kind. A continuous column on color is refused, and the message names size or opacity to show it instead:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + color(bronze)
data(medals) + text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) + color(col.bronze)
data(medals) + text + x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) +
  color(:bronze)
plot(data(medals), text, x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country),
  color(col.bronze))
Error:
! gog: `color(bronze)` maps a continuous (numeric) column, but `color` on `text` needs a categorical (text) column. Use `size` or `opacity` to show a continuous column.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

shape is refused outright, because it cannot change a string. A point’s glyph can change shape because the dot itself says nothing. A text mark’s glyph is the string itself, so there is nothing for shape to change:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + shape(country)
data(medals) + text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) + shape(col.country)
data(medals) + text + x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) +
  shape(:country)
plot(data(medals), text, x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country),
  shape(col.country))
Error:
! gog: `shape` cannot be bound to `text` — a text has no shape feature. Remove the `country` mapping from `shape`, or use a mark that maps it: `point`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

A string takes no texture either. pattern sets the texture of a stroke or of a filled region, and a word is neither:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) +
  style(pattern = "hatch")
(data(medals) + text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) +
  style(pattern = "hatch"))
data(medals) + text + x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) +
  style(pattern = "hatch")
plot(data(medals), text, x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country),
  style({ pattern: "hatch" }))
Error:
! gog: `style(pattern = )` sets a stroke pattern or a fill texture, and a `text` is neither a stroke nor a fill — a point's form is set by `shape`, a text's by its content. The strokes (`line`/`step`/`interval`/`path`/`rule`/`edge`) take a stroke pattern; the fills (`area`/`bar`/`box`/`ribbon`/`zone`) a fill texture.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

On a text layer, group splits the rows in three cases: a statistic summarizes them, dodge sets them side by side (Labels on dodged bars), or stack piles them up (Labels on stacked bars). A text layer with none of these draws one label for each row, so group has nothing to split. A scatter has no categorical axis, so it has no bars for the labels to be printed on, and gog suggests color instead:

  • R
  • Python
  • Julia
  • JavaScript
data(medals) + text + x(gold) + y(silver) + label(country) + group(country)
data(medals) + text + x(col.gold) + y(col.silver) + label(col.country) + group(col.country)
data(medals) + text + x(:gold) + y(:silver) + label(:country) +
  group(:country)
plot(data(medals), text, x(col.gold), y(col.silver), label(col.country),
  group(col.country))
Error:
! gog: `group` on a `text` needs `dodge`, `stack` or a statistic to act on, and on this plot none of them helps: there is no categorical axis whose bars the labels could be written on. Each row is already its own label, so splitting the rows by `country` would change nothing. To show the groups, map `country` to `color`.
gog: nothing was rendered. Fix the above, or set GOG_STRICT=0 to draw anyway.

16.16 In short

A text mark will not draw without a label, and no other mark accepts one. Its words come from a column, so a fixed note is a table with one row. repel draws every label and reports how many still overlap, because which names to leave out is your decision.

16.17 What comes next

Without repel, row order never moves a word: each one is drawn at the position its own row gives it. For a path, row order decides which rows are joined: the mark joins each row to the next, in the order the table holds them.
